specPoints.text: be able to use calculations and graphical methods to find the activation energy for a reaction from experimental data The Arrhenius equation will be given if needed.

primer.text: The rate constant k only stays constant while temperature is fixed. The Arrhenius equation links k to temperature, activation energy and the Arrhenius constant A. This note rearranges the relationship using natural logarithms, explains how a plot of ln k against 1/T gives a straight line whose gradient is -Ea/R, and works the standard activation-energy calculation from plotted data.

lessons.title: Temperature, the rate constant and the Arrhenius equation
lessons.opening: A rate equation keeps its k only while temperature holds still. Warm the mixture and a bigger fraction of collisions carries at least the activation energy, so both rate and k climb. The Arrhenius equation gathers the constants of a reaction into one expression that predicts exactly how strongly temperature moves k.
keyPoints: The rate constant k stays fixed only when concentration is the sole variable; changing temperature or the catalyst changes k.
At higher temperature a greater proportion of molecules possess energy at or above the activation energy.
Because rate and k are proportional to that energetic fraction, raising temperature raises both the rate and the rate constant.
The Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT) links k with temperature, with Ea and A characteristic of the reaction and R the universal gas constant.
In the Arrhenius equation only k and T vary; A varies negligibly with temperature and is treated as constant.

low.restatement: Heating shifts more molecules over the activation-energy bar, so k grows; the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT) puts that behaviour in one line.
low.analogy: A higher hurdle in a steeplechase lets fewer runners finish per minute; lower the hurdle or make the runners faster and more clear it.
low.examPointer: Quote k = A e^(-Ea/RT) and name every symbol - Ea, A, R and T - when you first use it.

medium.restatement: The exponential term e^(-Ea/RT) is the fraction of successful collisions; since it sits in both the rate expression and the definition of k, temperature moves the whole kinetic picture through one factor.
medium.analogy: A crowded club with a strict doorman: the fraction of hopefuls dressed for the theme (the energetic fraction) decides how fast the queue moves; relax the dress code (lower Ea) or excite the crowd (raise T) and entry speeds up.
medium.examPointer: Questions love the trap that k never changes: pin it down - k is temperature's prisoner.

options.explanation: Collision frequency rises too, but the decisive factor is the energetic fraction.

options.explanation: Heating does not create extra reactant.

options.text: Changes, because altering the catalyst is a condition change that k responds to
options.explanation: The Arrhenius picture treats catalyst identity as a condition that re-values k.

check.stem: State the Arrhenius equation and identify the constants in it.
check.modelAnswer: k = A e^(-Ea/RT), where Ea and A are constants characteristic of the reaction, R is the universal gas constant, and k and T are the variables.

check.stem: State what happens to the rate constant when temperature is raised, and why.
check.modelAnswer: The rate constant increases, because a greater proportion of molecules then hold energy at least equal to the activation energy, and k is proportional to that energetic fraction.

check.stem: Explain why raising the temperature raises the rate constant k.
check.modelAnswer: The rate constant is proportional to the fraction of molecules holding at least the activation energy; distributing molecular energies more widely at higher temperature enlarges that fraction, so k must rise with T.

check.stem: Two identical reactions run at 300 K and 320 K with the same Ea and A. Which run shows the larger k, and what does that predict for the observed rate?
check.modelAnswer: The 320 K run has the larger k because the exponential energetic fraction grows with T; since rate is proportional to k at fixed concentrations, the warmer mixture reacts measurably faster.

lessons.title: The logarithmic form and finding activation energy
lessons.opening: Taking natural logarithms turns the Arrhenius equation into a form built for calculation: ln k = ln A - Ea/RT. This lesson uses that line to reason about temperature changes, and then extracts an activation energy from measured k and T values in the standard exam calculation.
keyPoints: Natural logarithms convert the Arrhenius equation to ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT).
A temperature rise gives a greater ln k and therefore a greater k, so the reaction runs faster.
Raising the activation energy lowers the proportion of sufficiently energetic molecules, so k falls.
Measured pairs of k and T values let the activation energy be calculated, the most common exam task on this topic.
On a plot of ln k against 1/T the constant ln A becomes the intercept and -Ea/R the gradient.

low.restatement: The log form ln k = ln A - Ea/RT lets you solve straight for Ea from one k-T pair, and predicts that hotter means larger k.
low.analogy: A pay slip: gross pay (ln A) minus a deduction scaled by effort (Ea over RT) leaves the take-home figure (ln k); raise the effort charge and take-home shrinks.
low.examPointer: Rearrange as Ea = RT(ln A - ln k) before substituting, and keep R in J mol-1 K-1 with T in kelvin.

medium.restatement: Because ln k depends linearly on 1/T, every question about temperature effects reduces to reading one line: its slope is -Ea/R and its intercept is ln A.
medium.analogy: A ladder leaning against a wall: the lean of the ladder (the gradient) tells you the distance to the wall (Ea) without measuring it directly.
medium.examPointer: Check units at the end: Ea emerges in J mol-1, so convert to kJ mol-1 if the question expects it.

options.text: Unchanged, since Ea only affects the rate
options.explanation: k and the rate move together; both fall.

options.text: Finding the activation energy from measured k and T values
options.explanation: That is the standard exam task of this topic.

options.text: Measuring the orders m and n
options.explanation: Orders come from rate experiments, not the Arrhenius line.

options.text: Balancing the equation of the reaction
options.explanation: Nothing here involves balancing.
Half-life belongs to order analysis.

check.stem: In ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT), the constant ln A acts as

options.text: The intercept of the straight-line plot of ln k against 1/T
options.explanation: Setting 1/T to zero leaves ln k = ln A.
The gradient is -Ea/R.
That is Ea in the slope.
T sits in the x-variable 1/T.

check.stem: A reaction's k is measured at two temperatures. To extract Ea, you should

options.text: Apply Ea = RT(ln A - ln k) using the known A, or plot ln k against 1/T and use the gradient
options.explanation: Both routes come straight from the log form.

options.text: Average the two k values and multiply by R
options.explanation: No averaging law exists here.
Squaring k has no basis in the equation.

options.text: Substitute the temperatures into the rate equation
options.explanation: The rate equation carries orders, not Ea.

check.stem: Write the logarithmic form of the Arrhenius equation.
check.modelAnswer: ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT), where each symbol keeps its Arrhenius meaning.

check.stem: State the effect on k of raising temperature and of raising activation energy.
check.modelAnswer: Raising temperature increases k; raising activation energy decreases k.

check.stem: Explain why the logarithmic form is easier to use for calculations than the original exponential equation.
check.modelAnswer: The log form is linear in the variables: ln k depends on 1/T through the single constant combination Ea/R, so an unknown such as Ea can be isolated and solved algebraically instead of un-doing an exponential.

check.stem: A student computes Ea from two k-T pairs but reports it in J mol-1 while the mark scheme expects kJ mol-1. What went wrong and what is the fix?
check.modelAnswer: Nothing is wrong except the unit presentation: with R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1 the arithmetic returns joules, so the student should divide by 1000 to express the answer in kJ mol-1.

lessons.title: Reading Ea and A from an Arrhenius plot
lessons.opening: Plotted as ln k against 1/T, the Arrhenius equation becomes the straight line y = mx + c with gradient -Ea/R and intercept ln A. This lesson walks the full plotting routine: convert each k to ln k and each T to 1/T, plot, read the gradient, then lift Ea and A from the line.
keyPoints: When ln k is plotted against 1/T, the Arrhenius relation appears as a straight line; its slope carries -Ea/R.
The plotted line takes the y = mx + c form, with intercept equal to ln A.
The activation energy follows from the gradient: Ea = -gradient x R.
The Arrhenius constant follows from the intercept: A = e^(intercept).
Table completion, plotting and gradient reading are the practical steps of the method.

low.restatement: Plot ln k against 1/T: the straight line's gradient is -Ea/R and its intercept is ln A, so both Ea and A come off the graph.
low.analogy: A taxi fare chart: the flat starting fee is the intercept and the per-kilometre charge is the gradient; read both off the printed line.
low.examPointer: Watch the sign: a negative gradient means Ea comes out positive once you multiply by -R.

medium.restatement: Every point on the plot is one experiment; the collective slope averages the whole data set, which is why graphical Ea values are preferred over single-pair arithmetic.
medium.analogy: Judging a team from its season-long trend rather than one match: the line through all the points is fairer than any single result.
medium.examPointer: If asked for A, do not stop at Ea - the intercept still needs converting with e^(intercept).

check.stem: State the gradient and the intercept of the ln k against 1/T plot.
check.modelAnswer: The gradient is -Ea/R and the intercept is ln A.

check.stem: State the two conversions applied to raw k and T data before plotting.
check.modelAnswer: Each rate constant is converted to ln k, and each temperature to the reciprocal 1/T.

check.stem: Explain why the Arrhenius plot gives a straight line.
check.modelAnswer: Taking logarithms removes the exponential, leaving ln k as a linear function of 1/T with fixed coefficients ln A and -Ea/R, so plotting one against the other must produce a straight line.

check.stem: A student's plotted line has intercept 30.2. Report A and comment on its size.
check.modelAnswer: A = e^(30.2), roughly 1.3 x 10^13, an enormous pre-exponential factor typical of gas-phase reactions where the steric factor multiplies collision frequency into a very large constant.

glossary.definition: The factor k in a rate equation, re-valued whenever temperature or catalyst changes.
The minimum energy Ea that colliding molecules must carry for reaction to occur.
The pre-exponential factor A, characteristic of a reaction and effectively temperature-independent.
A plot of ln k versus 1/T: its slope, -Ea/R, and its intercept, ln A, give Ea and A.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the activation energy of a reaction taking place at 400 K whose rate constant is 6.25 x 10^-4 s^-1, given A = 4.6 x 10^13 and R = 8.31 J mol^-1 K^-1.
steps: Rearrange the log form ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT) to make Ea the subject: Ea = RT(ln A - ln k).
Evaluate the logarithms: ln(6.25 x 10^-4) = -7.378 and ln(4.6 x 10^13) = 31.460.
Multiply through: 8.31 x 400 = 3324, and 3324 x 38.837 = 129,080 J mol^-1.
Round and convert: about 129 kJ mol^-1.
